title: Two Eyes
intro: You know that a group dies when its last liberty is filled. So here is the question that follows from it, and it is the most important question in Go.
How does a group become impossible to kill?
Not hard to kill. Impossible. There is an answer and it is exact.

steps.instruction: That black group surrounds three empty points in a row. Play the middle one.
steps.hint: The middle of the three. Yes, inside your own shape.
steps.explanation: Two separate empty points, each surrounded entirely by your own stones. Those are eyes. White cannot play either one -- each would be a stone with no liberties -- and White cannot fill both at once, because filling one is illegal while the other is still there.

steps.instruction: This black group has one eye and nothing else. You are White. Take it.
steps.hint: The group is touching exactly one empty point. It is inside.
steps.explanation: One eye is not life. The eye was the group's last liberty, so playing in it was legal -- the capture is resolved before your own stone is checked. Everything a beginner believes about eyes stops here.

steps.instruction: The same group, with two eyes instead of one. Try to take it the same way.
steps.hint: Play in one of the eyes. The game will stop you.
steps.explanation: Refused, and by the ordinary rule rather than a special one. Your stone would have no liberties, and it captures nothing, because the group still has the other eye. That is what alive means: not difficult to kill, but not killable at all.

outro: Two eyes lives. One eye dies. Every life-and-death problem ever set is that sentence, wearing a disguise.
When you are next unsure whether a group is in trouble, do not count its liberties. Count its eyes.
